result: BtaR1 mutants have a fitness advantage over wild-type in broth coculture, rising from 1% to 50% of the population after 3 days, while BtaR2 and BtaR3 mutants show no such advantage. This fitness advantage is attributed to the metabolic cost of the larger BtaR1 regulon (>150 genes) compared to the smaller BtaR2 and BtaR3 regulons.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as 'straightforward and interesting' without raising concerns about the broth competition data or the interpretation of metabolic costs. The summary confirms 'the main new finding' builds on this observation.

result: In contrast to broth cocultures, BtaR1 mutants show no fitness advantage on agar plate cocultures, remaining at ~1% of the population after four daily transfers. BtaR2 and BtaR3 mutants similarly show no fitness disadvantage on agar plates.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these agar surface competition results. They requested figure improvements (keys, legends) but accepted the underlying data showing contact-dependent constraint of BtaR1 mutants.

result: Quorum sensing activates T6SS-1 toxin-immunity genes (including tle1/tli1 and paralogs) in B. thailandensis, though the T6SS-1 apparatus genes themselves are not QS-controlled. Analysis of transcriptomics data identified 9 T6SS-1 substrate genes and 8 additional related genes activated by QS.
evaluation: Reviewers noted 'it is not clear if one or more T6SS toxin/immunity genes is directly involved' and requested ectopic expression experiments with immunity genes to clarify which specific toxin/immunity pairs mediate the policing effect. Figure 2A was criticized as 'so compressed that little useful information is presented.'

result: Wild-type B. thailandensis outcompetes T6SS-1 effector/immunity mutants, while BtaR1 mutants show impaired inhibition of these mutants. BtaR2 and BtaR3 mutants retain wild-type levels of inhibition. The authors propose this killing defect results from inability to fully activate T6S toxin gene expression.
evaluation: Reviewers requested an additional control for Figure 2B: 'An appropriate control would have been to use a Type VI mutant as the inhibitor versus the tle1 mutant to demonstrate it no longer inhibits growth.' This suggests the evidence for the mechanism is incomplete.

result: T6SS-1 is required to constrain BtaR1 mutants during agar surface growth. In competitions between T6SS-1 mutants and BtaR1-T6SS-1 double mutants, the double mutant rises to ~25% on agar but shows fitness advantage in broth. Complementation with clpV restores constraint, demonstrating dependence on an intact T6SS-1 apparatus.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these genetic complementation experiments without specific critique. They requested figure improvements (keys, reproducibility information) but did not question the conclusion that T6SS-1 mediates contact-dependent constraint.

result: Quorum sensing activates T6SS-1 growth inhibition to police and constrain quorum-sensing mutants in B. thailandensis, defining a novel role for T6SSs in intraspecies mutant control. This represents a mechanism by which wild-type populations mitigate the cost of QS gene regulation.
evaluation: Reviewers summarized this as 'the main new finding of this study' and found it 'straightforward and interesting.' They accepted the policing interpretation, though they requested clarification of which specific toxin/immunity genes are involved.

result: The BtaR1-BtaI1 QS system carries a metabolic cost evident in broth culture competitions and growth curves. BtaR1 mutants outcompete wild-type in broth presumably because no cell contact occurs and there is a cost associated with QS gene activation.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the metabolic cost interpretation or the speculation about lack of cell contact in broth. They accepted this as part of the overall model without requesting additional evidence.

result: The BtaR2-BtaI2 and BtaR3-BtaI3 QS systems do not appear to carry the large metabolic cost associated with BtaR1-BtaI1.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question this inference, which is based on the lack of fitness effects for BtaR2 and BtaR3 mutants in both broth and agar competitions.
